title: Comparatives: irregular farther/further
question: The shop is ___ than I thought.
explanation: 'Far' has irregular comparatives: far, farther (or further). We never say 'more far'. 'Farthest' is a superlative and 'far' is the base form.

title: Comparatives: as...as
question: My brother is ___ tall as my father.
explanation: We use 'as...as' to show two things are equal: He is as tall as my father. 'More tall as', 'that tall as', and 'much tall as' are all ungrammatical.

title: Comparatives: negative as...as
question: This test was not ___ difficult as the last one.
explanation: In negative comparisons, we say 'not as...as'. 'Not so much difficult as', 'not more difficult as', and 'not than difficult as' are all ungrammatical.

title: Comparatives: double comparative
question: The days are getting ___.
explanation: We use 'comparative + and + comparative' to show something is increasing: longer and longer. 'More longer' is a double comparative (ungrammatical).

title: Comparatives: double comparative (long adj)
question: The city is becoming ___.
explanation: For long adjectives, we repeat 'more': more and more expensive. The adjective is not repeated on its own, and 'most' is a superlative.

title: Comparatives: the...the
question: ___ you practice, the better you get.
explanation: We use 'the + comparative, the + comparative' to show connected changes: The more...the better. 'More you practice', 'Much more you practice', and 'The much you practice' are ungrammatical at the start of this construction.

title: Comparatives: irregular worse
question: His handwriting is ___ than mine.
explanation: 'Bad' has an irregular comparative: bad → worse. 'Worser', 'badder', and 'more bad' are not correct.

title: Comparatives: less
question: This movie is ___ exciting than the book.
explanation: 'Less' is the opposite of 'more' for adjective comparisons: less exciting. 'Lesser', 'fewer', and 'littler' do not work before an adjective here.

title: Superlatives: irregular least
question: That was the ___ useful advice I've ever received.
explanation: The superlative of 'little' (in quantity) is 'least': the least useful. 'Less', 'most little', and 'littlest' are ungrammatical here.

title: Superlatives: one of the + plural
question: She is one of the ___ in her class.
explanation: After 'one of the + superlative', we need a plural noun. 'Tallest student' (singular) and 'taller students' (not superlative) are ungrammatical in this frame.

title: First conditional: unless (means 'if not')
question: You won't pass the exam ___ you study harder.
explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not'. 'If you study harder' would give the opposite meaning, and 'because' and 'although' do not express the condition 'if not'.

title: First conditional: in case (precaution)
question: Take an umbrella ___ it rains later.
explanation: 'In case' means 'as a precaution for a possible future event'. 'So', 'then' and 'while' cannot join the two clauses with this meaning.

title: First conditional: as long as (condition)
question: You can borrow my car ___ you drive carefully.
explanation: 'As long as' is a conjunction meaning 'on the condition that'. 'As far as', 'as well as' and 'as if' have other meanings.

title: First conditional: provided that
question: I'll lend you the money ___ you pay me back next week.
explanation: 'Provided that' is a conjunction meaning 'only if'. 'Provide' is a verb, and 'provided with' and 'provided of' do not introduce a condition.

title: First conditional: when vs if
question: I'll call you ___ I arrive. I'm sure I will get there at six.
explanation: Use 'when' for something you are sure will happen, and 'if' for something that may or may not happen. 'Unless' means 'if not' and 'although' shows contrast.

title: First conditional: even if (no matter what)
question: I'll go for a run ___ it's freezing outside.
explanation: 'Even if' means 'no matter whether': I'll go running whatever the weather. 'Even so', 'as if' and 'if only' do not join the clauses with this meaning.

title: First conditional: otherwise
question: Hurry up. ___, we will miss the bus.
explanation: 'Otherwise' means 'if you don't': Hurry up. Otherwise, we will miss the bus. 'Unless', 'although' and 'because' need a clause after them, not a comma.

title: First conditional: verb after 'if'
question: If you ___ your homework, I'll let you play outside.
explanation: After 'if' in a first conditional, use the present simple: If you finish. 'Will finish' is not used in the 'if' clause, and 'finished' and 'finishing' are the wrong form.

title: First conditional: verb after 'unless'
question: 'Unless it ___ tomorrow, we will have a picnic.' Which is correct?
explanation: After 'unless', use the present simple, not 'will' or 'would'. 'Rain' does not agree with 'it'.

title: First conditional: 'in case' fixed form
question: I'll pack snacks now ___ we get hungry on the hike.
explanation: 'In case' takes a clause directly: 'in case we get hungry'. 'In the case' and 'in case of' need a noun, and 'in case if' repeats the idea of 'if'.

title: Adverbs: good vs well
question: She sings very ___.
explanation: 'Good' is an adjective; 'well' is the adverb needed after the verb 'sings'. 'Better' and 'best' cannot follow 'very'.

title: Adverbs: hard vs hardly
question: He works very ___ at his job.
explanation: 'Hard' is both an adjective and an adverb ('work hard'). 'Hardly' means 'almost not', 'harder' and 'hardest' cannot follow 'very'.

title: Adverbs: hard vs hardly (meaning)
question: I ___ know him. We only met once.
explanation: 'Hardly' means 'almost not'. 'Hard', 'harder', and 'hardest' cannot precede 'know him' here; they are ungrammatical in this slot.

title: Adverbs: late vs lately
question: She has been feeling tired ___.
explanation: 'Lately' means recently. 'Late' means after the expected time, 'later' means afterwards and 'last' means final; none fits after 'feeling tired'.

title: Adverbs: position with verbs
question: She ___ forgotten to call me.
explanation: Adverbs go between the auxiliary and the main verb: has probably forgotten. 'Probable' is an adjective and cannot modify a verb; 'probably have' shows wrong agreement with 'she'.

title: Adverbs: position with be
question: The children are ___ quiet today.
explanation: Before an adjective, we need an adverb: unusually quiet. 'Unusual' is an adjective and cannot modify 'quiet'; 'more unusual' and 'most unusual' are comparative and superlative adjectives.

title: Adverbs: adjective vs adverb
question: He drove ___ through the storm.
explanation: We need an adverb to describe HOW he drove. 'Careful' is an adjective, and 'more careful' and 'most careful' are comparative and superlative adjectives that cannot modify the verb 'drove'.

title: Adverbs: near vs nearly
question: I ___ missed my flight. I arrived just in time.
explanation: 'Nearly' means 'almost'. 'Near' and 'nearby' describe place, and 'nearer' is a comparative; none can come before 'missed'.

title: Adverbs: fast (no -ly)
question: She runs very ___.
explanation: 'Fast' is both an adjective and an adverb. 'Fastly' is not a word; 'more fast' is ungrammatical (use 'faster'); 'very fastest' is ungrammatical (very + superlative).

title: Adverbs: already position
question: We have ___ eaten dinner.
explanation: 'Already' goes between the auxiliary and the main verb: have already eaten. 'Yet' is for negatives and questions, 'ago' follows a time, and 'soon' refers to the future.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: stop + gerund (quit)
question: He stopped ___ because the doctor told him to quit.
explanation: 'Stop + gerund' means to quit an activity. 'To smoke' would mean he paused in order to smoke, which does not fit the doctor's advice.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: stop + infinitive (pause)
question: She was thirsty, so she stopped ___ a coffee on her way to work.
explanation: 'Stop + to-infinitive' means you paused one action in order to do another. 'Buying' would mean she quit buying coffee, which does not fit 'thirsty'.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: remember + gerund (memory)
question: I remember ___ the door before I left. I can see myself doing it.
explanation: 'Remember + gerund' expresses a memory of a past action. 'Remember to lock' would mean not forgetting a task.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: remember + infinitive (task)
question: Please remember ___ the lights when you leave.
explanation: 'Remember + to-infinitive' = a task to do. 'Turning off' would be the memory of doing it, and the other forms are ungrammatical here.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: try + gerund (experiment)
question: The room was hot, so I tried ___ the window. It helped a lot!
explanation: 'Try + gerund' means you experiment with a solution: tried opening the window. The other forms are ungrammatical after 'tried' in this slot.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: try + infinitive (attempt)
question: I tried ___ the heavy box, but I wasn't strong enough.
explanation: 'Try + to-infinitive' means you attempted something difficult: tried to lift the box. The other forms are ungrammatical after 'tried' here.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: forget + gerund (memory)
question: I'll never forget ___ Paris for the first time.
explanation: 'Forget + gerund' = the memory of a past experience. 'To visit' would mean failing to do a task.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: forget + infinitive (task)
question: Don't forget ___ milk on the way home.
explanation: 'Forget + to-infinitive' = fail to do a future task: Don't forget to buy milk. 'Buying' would be a memory of a past action.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: keep
question: He kept ___ about the noise, but nobody listened.
explanation: 'Keep' is always followed by a gerund: kept complaining. It is never followed by an infinitive or a bare verb.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: refuse
question: She refused ___ the money, even though she needed it.
explanation: 'Refuse' is always followed by a to-infinitive: refused to take. It is never followed by a gerund or a bare verb.

title: Too/enough: too + adjective + to
question: This coffee is too hot ___.
explanation: 'Too + adjective + to-infinitive': too hot to drink. The other forms are ungrammatical in this slot.

title: Too/enough: enough + for
question: Is this room big ___ for twenty people?
explanation: 'Enough' goes after the adjective: big enough. 'Too', 'very' and 'so' cannot follow 'big' in this position.

title: Too/enough: enough + noun
question: Do we have enough ___ to make dinner?
explanation: 'Enough' goes directly before an uncountable noun: enough food. 'Of food' and 'the food' cannot follow 'enough', and 'much food' adds an extra quantifier.

title: Too/enough: enough + to
question: She is old enough ___ a car.
explanation: 'Adjective + enough + to-infinitive': old enough to drive. The other forms are ungrammatical here.

title: Too/enough: too + to
question: He is too young ___ alone at night.
explanation: 'Too + adjective + to-infinitive': too young to go out. The other forms are ungrammatical here.

title: Too/enough: too few
question: There are too ___ students in the class, so we need more.
explanation: 'Few' is used with countable plural nouns: too few students means not enough. 'Little' and 'less' are for uncountable nouns, and 'fewer' cannot follow 'too'.

title: Too/enough: too little
question: I have too ___ money to buy a car.
explanation: 'Little' is used with uncountable nouns: too little money means not enough. 'Few' is for countable nouns, and 'small' and 'less' cannot follow 'too' here.

title: Too/enough: not enough + noun
question: There aren't enough ___ for everyone.
explanation: 'Not enough + plural countable noun': not enough chairs. 'Of chairs', 'chair' and 'a chair' cannot follow 'enough' here.

title: Too/enough: enough position
question: The box is light ___ for me to carry.
explanation: After an adjective with 'for me to carry', only 'enough' fits. 'Light too for me to carry', 'light so for me to carry', and 'light very for me to carry' are all ungrammatical (these words precede the adjective).

title: Too/enough: too...to vs enough...to
question: She spoke too quickly for me ___. Can you repeat it?
explanation: 'Too + adverb + for someone + to-infinitive': too quickly for me to understand. The other forms are ungrammatical here.
